question: Why does an order wait, when does it expire, and how is it cancelled?
title: Order lifecycle
summary: An order waits when its items are short or earlier orders wait for the same items; the worker admits it later, in order. It expires a day after it was placed at most; when it does, or the customer cancels, the order is marked cancelling and the worker voids the charge and releases the stock.

steps.title: The page sends a dry run before the real order

anchor.after:

steps.lead: Before the customer is sent to their bank, the page sends the order as a dry run. Stock and prices are checked; a back-ordered item is reported, not refused.
steps.details: The real POST follows in the same function. The page waits at most 10 minutes for the payment (`timeoutMs` in `web/src/checkout/Checkout.vue`), the order itself waits longer.

steps.title: Back-ordered items make the order wait instead of failing

steps.lead: The API runs the stock check on the order before storing it. If an item is back-ordered, the order is still stored, with a reason and a message saying it waits.
steps.details: The dry run answers with the same message, so the page can say "back-ordered" before the customer pays anything. Nothing is reserved here: the worker reserves later.

steps.title: The API previews the stock check, so a waiting order says so

anchor.before: // Preview gives the same verdict for an order that is not stored yet; it stores nothing.

steps.lead: `Preview` is the worker's stock check on an order that is not stored yet. It reads the open orders and the stock levels and stores nothing.
steps.details: The message gets a "Some items are back-ordered" prefix so the customer reads it as a delay, not an error. The worker repeats the same check for real on its next pass.

steps.lead: Every order gets an `expiresAt` when it is stored: the shop's order TTL, never more than 24 hours. A back-ordered order also gets its stock reason here.
steps.details: The cap lives in `expiry`; an order waiting for stock still expires, so a customer is never charged days later for an order they forgot.

steps.lead: Nothing notifies the worker: every 2 s each phase lists the open orders and handles them one after another, each with its own 30 s timeout.
steps.details: `Run` starts one loop per phase (orders, expire). The interval is set in `cmd/shop/main.go`. A slow provider call holds up only the orders behind it in this pass.

steps.lead: Orders are sorted by creation time; only earlier orders that wait for stock and share an item count as ahead. Waiting never moves an order back.
steps.details: The order keeps its `CreatedAt` while it waits, so it stays ahead of orders placed after it.

steps.lead: For each line the check compares the warehouse's count minus what other open orders reserved with the quantity ordered, then asks who is ahead.
steps.details: A discontinued item can never be filled; a short count only means waiting. The levels and reservations come from the warehouse in two reads.

steps.title: Never available: it fails at once. Short or queued: it waits

anchor.after: // stockCheck gathers what the decision needs: what the order wants, what the warehouse holds, what earlier

steps.lead: `admit` turns the verdict into a stored decision: failed for an item that is no longer sold, a stock reason and message for an order that must wait.
steps.details: Only an order with nothing in its way goes on to be charged, with its reason cleared. A waiting order is checked again on every pass.

steps.lead: A pending order that passes `admit` reserves its items, gets its charge and becomes `charging`; its payment deadline starts now, not at creation.
steps.details: A sold-out item at reservation time fails the order before anyone is charged. A passing provider error sends it to `retryLater` instead of failing it.

steps.title: A charge refused for now goes back to pending, keeping its place

anchor.before:
// retryLater puts back an order whose charge the provider refused for a passing reason (rate limit, maintenance):
// its stock is released, it goes back to pending and it keeps its place in the stock queue.

steps.lead: When the provider refuses a charge for a passing reason, the reservation is released and the order goes back to pending with a provider reason.
steps.details: It keeps its creation time, so it is first in line again among orders for the same items. After five retries it fails for good.

steps.title: A database-only loop marks expired orders as cancelling

anchor.before:
// expire marks an unpaid order past its expiry as cancelling. It reads and writes the database only, so orders
// still expire while the payment provider is down.
anchor.after: // orderStage works out what the customer is waiting for, from what the provider says about the charge.

steps.lead: The expire phase reads and writes the database only: an unpaid order past its `expiresAt` is marked cancelling, whatever the payment provider is doing.
steps.details: The worker carries out the cancel on its next orders pass, the same way as a cancel from the customer. It also triggers the clean-up of abandoned reservations.

steps.title: Cancel only sets the same cancelling status on the order

anchor.before:
return
	}

steps.lead: The cancel endpoint changes no stock and calls no provider: it marks the order cancelling and answers 202. A paid order is refunded instead.

steps.title: Cancelling voids the charge, then releases the stock

anchor.before: return applyOutcome(ctx, w.Store, o, stage, waiting, issues)

steps.lead: For a cancelling order the worker voids the charge first, so the customer is never charged for an order that no longer exists, then releases the stock.
steps.details: A charge that already settled is not an error here; the refund flow handles it. Only when both are done does the order become cancelled.

steps.title: Every 10 min, reservations without an open order are released

steps.lead: Reservations whose order no longer exists (deleted by hand, a crash between reserving and storing) are released, at most every 10 minutes.
steps.details: A reservation younger than an hour is left alone, so an order being stored right now is not robbed of its stock.
